newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Bank sees good medium-term growth in North Africa.
newsitem.headline: Bank sees good medium-term growth in North Africa.

text.p: The Maghreb states of North Africa are expected to record strong medium-term growth, with Tunisia leading on an average 6.5 percent annually in 1996-2000, the African Development Bank (AfDB) said.
But the economies of the five North African Arab states are constrained by political or climatic problems, AfDB said in a report released at the weekend.
"The projected growth rate for Algeria during the forecast period is 5.4 percent per annum," said the bank's "African Development Report, 1996".
"The economy of Egypt remains sound and as long as the political situation remains stable, it is anticipated to continue to expand at a forecast rate of 4.7 percent per annum."
During the 1996-2000 period, Morocco is projected to grow at an average 5.4 percent, according to AfDB, the premier development institution for the world's poorest continent.

Morocco, and to a lesser extent Tunisia, are the victims of recurrent drought. Libya is under U.N. sanctions for its alleged role in the terrorist bombing of a U.S. airliner in 1988 which killed 270 people.
The report made no growth forecast for Libya. A senior AfDB official said this was due to uncertainty as to how long Libya would remain under sanctions.
Other independent sources estimate Libya, Africa's second largest oil exporter in the OPEC group, would grow at an average 3.6 percent in the same forecast period.
The governments of both Egypt and Algeria are battling armed Islamic fundamentalist opponents. In the case of Egypt the violence has devastated its vital tourist industry.
Tunisia and Morocco remain the success stories of the region owing to their implementation of economic reforms "early and in a sustained manner", the bank said.

"One problem facing these two economies is the sporadic drought which afflicts the region. Morocco went through another drought in 1995, having just emerged from one two years previously," the report said.

"These two economies remain dependent on agriculture and any factors affecting this sector also affect the rest of the economy. However, in a few years and with the development of the manufacturing sector, particularly in Tunisia, the vulnerability of these economies to climatic circumstances will be reduced," it said.
AfDB forecast that, in the near to medium term, Morocco and Tunisia should fare very well in overcoming any adverse weather developments.
